name: austin
desc: Python frame stack sampler for CPython
why: A sampling profiler that watches a running CPython process from outside without modifying it, a neat way to see execution.

brief.what_it_is: Austin is a frame stack sampler for CPython, written in pure C. It reads the CPython interpreter's memory from outside the process to find the running threads and the stack of frames each one is executing, at a regular interval (default 100 microseconds). Input is a running or launched Python process; output is binary MOJO data (or collapsed stacks, Speedscope JSON, or pprof after conversion) that can be piped into flame graph and profiling tools. The README also describes a live terminal view (-w) that prints current thread stacks.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a profiler that needs no instrumentation and has minimal impact on the target: 'Hence, one can use Austin to easily make powerful statistical profilers that have minimal impact on the target application and that don't require any instrumentation.' Its pitch is that it is 'Just a sampler', leaving analysis to other tools.
brief.how_it_works: Samples are collected by reading the CPython interpreter's virtual memory space to retrieve information about the currently running threads and their frame stacks. Austin dumps raw stacks at intervals and leaves aggregation to later tools, which the README says lets it sample faster than tools that aggregate at run time. The optional austinp variant instead uses ptrace and libunwind to capture native stacks, at a higher impact on the target.

brief.install_notes: Linux: the only build dependency is the standard C library. Build from source with ./configure, make, make install after autoreconf --install, or compile directly with gcc -O3 -Os -Wall -pthread src/*.c -o src/austin. Attaching to external processes needs sudo or the CAP_SYS_PTRACE capability; in Docker, start the container with --cap-add SYS_PTRACE. macOS: attaching needs sudo, and the system Python and python.org installers are blocked by System Integrity Protection and the Hardened Runtime unless the python binary's signature is removed; pyenv, Anaconda and Homebrew Python work out of the box. Windows: compile with gcc -O3 -Os -Wall -lpsapi -lntdll src/*.c -o src/austin, or install with choco install austin or scoop install austin. Conda users can run conda install -c conda-forge austin. The austin-tui module needs python-curses, which the README says is broken in standard Windows Python builds. Austin supports CPython 3.9 through 3.14.
brief.standout: Austin is a sampler with no instrumentation and no run-time aggregation: it writes raw stacks in a compact binary format and leaves analysis to converters and viewers such as FlameGraph, Speedscope, pprof, a VS Code extension and a TUI. It also attaches to a running process (including child processes and sub-interpreters) and can sample garbage collector state.
brief.status: Appears maintained. The README lists support for CPython 3.9 through 3.14 and mentions Austin 4.0.0 and 3.x release features, with CI badges and a latest-release badge. I could not see a release date or last commit date in the fetched text, so recent activity is unconfirmed.
brief.caveats: Licensed GPLv3, per the badge in the README. Linux attach needs root or CAP_SYS_PTRACE. macOS attach needs sudo and fails for SIP- or hardened-runtime-protected Python builds, such as the system Python and python.org installers. The austinp native-stack variant uses ptrace, so its impact on the target is no longer minimal and it is not recommended in production; its default interval is 10 ms. Austin writes binary data, so the README warns to use -o or redirect output to a file. Logs go to syslog on Linux and macOS, and to %TEMP%\austin.log on Windows. The Windows curses problem affects the TUI only.
